doc.title: Frank Tate interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Cannonball and Nancy Wilson on Capitol; a Zawinul trio record
summary: Rowe and Tate share love of the Cannonball and Nancy Wilson album and discuss pop turns by record companies.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: The reason I lit up is because my favorite album in the whole world is Cannonball and Nancy Wilson, on Capitol.
Oh sure, yeah. They do “Happy Talk” and —
“Save Your Love for Me.”
Yeah. With the quintet, with Nat and Lou Hayes and
Joe Zawinul.

Zawinul, excuse me, Zawinul. I have a trio record of his called “To You With Love” that was purchased at the Tate Street Drug Store in 1963 for a dollar. It’s on a label called Strand. And Louis Porter, who has everything ever — you know Louis?
Um hum. I don’t know him but I know who he is.
He found the record, it’s in a catalog that’s Joe Zawinul playing straight ahead, no funk, no rock & roll, acoustic piano trio record. Are we up again?
[Monk, you talk]
I’m talking. Yeah I’m a real Cannonball nut.
[okay]
And just that record just is it for me, Perfect.
Yeah I thought that was the best material she ever did. You know record companies they get into somebody.
Yeah and she took heat for it too she told me.

I’m sure she did. Cannonball must have taken heat for “Mercy, Mercy, Mercy” and all that stuff. I mean I don’t know the record business you know. I don’t know how these characters operate at the desk you know, but these guys they get an advance and then they’ve got to sell records. And Cannonball started doing all that pop music and Nancy
Wilson did a record where there was a tune on there called “It’s All Over Mr. Walker I Don’t Want the New York Secretary’s Life.” A country & western tune.
Wow.
So I mean I doubt that was a, you know, but I heard when you know.
And you saw her when.
I saw her, yeah, I sure did.
